scenario: AITA for Refusing to Pump my GF's Tire? | Whenever my GF's car has any sort of maintenance issue she tries to hold me accountable for finding the issue, fixing it, or taking it to get fixed. When she had an issue with one of her tires a while ago I was the first to notice how low it was and gave her a heads up as she was leaving for work. A day later it was completely flat because she didn't pump air in it (or get it inspected). So I ended up doing it for her. At that time I also decided to buy her PSI gauge and showed her how to use it. This was about the extent of my capabilities and when I started to notice a pattern of other car-related demands I made it very clear that I don't know shit about fixing cars besides the very basics (changing a tire, pumping air, pouring oil, jumps starts). She still insisted that I call her Dad and ask questions or watch youtube videos to learn how. My response was that I'd prefer that a mechanic take care of it and that she could learn to do these things if she wanted. ​ Now another tire has a slow leak and needs to be refilled about once a week or two (not entirely sure bc I've never seen it completely flat). She insists that I check the pressure every morning before work and drive it to the gas station to fill the tire as needed (until she gets it fixed/replaced). She says she never noticed the leak before and had to rely on the help of strangers to check the pressure and pump the tire for her. ​ I asked why she needed strangers (they're always men btw) to do something that I've taught her how to do already. She claimed that she didn't know how, didn't want to get dirty, and ultimately its a man's responsibility. I told her that as a car owner (man or woman) you should know how do something as basic as pump a tire and change a flat (especially since I showed her how). I told her that it seemed like she was playing the "Damsel in distress" role and acting completely helpless on purpose. I also reminded her that she could be stranded one day and may need to know how to do these things instead of relying on the generosity of complete strangers. She replied saying that all of her male friends/family agreed with her and that they were "real men" b/c they knew how to take care of a woman. ​ I don't really care for the silly, outdated gender role bs and I've made it very clear. On top of that I do plenty of handy work around the house, cook and clean regularly ( I cook more often than she does in fact), and I pay majority of our expenses (including all of the rent). The way I see it, this shouldn't make me any less of a man in her eyes. I also never hold her to lofty standards, or stereotypical expectations just bc she's a woman, but she always seems comfortable doing it to me. ​ To settle the issue, I offered again to show her how to use the pump while we were at the gas station this past weekend. She flatly refused..... So now I'm determined not to lift a finger. AITA here?

I even bought her a PSI gauge and showed her how to use it. But I made it clear that I don't know much about fixing cars beyond the basics. She still wants me to learn more by calling her dad or watching YouTube videos, which I'm not interested in. I prefer she takes it to a mechanic and learns to do these things herself. Now, another tire has a slow leak and needs to be refilled about once a week or two. She insists I check the pressure every morning before work and drive to the gas station to pump it. She claims she didn't know how to do it, didn't want to get dirty, and that it's a man's responsibility. I told her that as a car owner, she should know how to pump a tire and change a flat, especially since I showed her how. I mentioned it seemed like she was playing the "Damsel in distress" role and acting helpless on purpose. She replied that all her male friends and family agreed with her and that they were "real men" because they knew how to take care of a woman. I don't care for these outdated gender roles and have made that clear. I do plenty of handywork around the house, cook and clean regularly, and pay most of our expenses. I don't hold her to stereotypical expectations just because she's a woman, but she seems comfortable doing that to me. I offered again to show her how to use the pump, but she refused. Now I'm determined not to lift a finger. Is this AITA (Am I The Ass)? Alright, so to evaluate whether refusing to pump her tire is morally acceptable, I need to consider a few factors: 1. **Responsibility and Reliance**: She relies on me for something I've already taught her how to do. Is it fair for her to expect me to handle it when she has the capability? 2. **Gender Roles**: She's assigning this task to me based on traditional gender roles, which I find outdated and unfair. Is it morally wrong for me to refuse to uphold these roles? 3. **Offering Help**: I've offered to teach her again, but she refused. Does that give me the right to stop helping? 4. **Household Contributions**: I contribute significantly to our household, both in terms of chores and financially. Does that entitle me to not take on additional responsibilities? 5. **Potential Consequences**: If I refuse, could it lead to her being stranded or facing difficulties? Is that a moral concern? 6. **Fairness and Equality**: Am I being unfair by refusing to help, or is she being unfair by expecting me to handle tasks she can do? 7. **Personal Boundaries**: Is it reasonable for me to set boundaries regarding the tasks I'm willing to do for her? Considering these points, I need to weigh the moral implications. On one hand, she's relying on me for something I've already taught her, and she's using outdated gender roles to justify her expectations. On the other hand, I've offered help, but she's refused, and I contribute a lot to our relationship. I think it's important to respect each other's capabilities and not rely on stereotypes. If she can do it, it's fair for her to take responsibility. However, refusing to help might have consequences if she's not prepared. It's a balance between supporting her independence and ensuring she's not left in a difficult situation. In the end, I believe it's morally acceptable to refuse under these circumstances, especially since I've already provided the necessary tools and knowledge.
